name: Pivot - Host Discovery Ping Sweep
command: for i in {1..254}; do (ping -c 1 172.16.5.$i | grep "bytes from" &); done
description: Once on a pivot, sweep the internal subnet for live hosts using native tools so you do not need to upload a scanner. Variations cover a Linux for-loop, Windows CMD, PowerShell, and the Metasploit ping_sweep post module.
source: CPTS Module 12: Pivoting, Tunneling, and Port Forwarding

examples.label: OSCP Ch18 - nc port-check loop to discover hosts with SMB open (seq variant)
examples.command: for i in $(seq 1 254); do nc -zv -w 1 172.16.50.$i 445; done 2>&1 | grep succeeded

notes: Sweep the pivot host's internal subnet to find live hosts (`post/multi/gather/ping_sweep`, or a for-loop over the range) once autoroute is set - your first discovery step on the new network segment. Also covered in: OSCP PEN-200 Chapter 18 (Port Redirection and SSH Tunneling). OSCP Ch18: nc -zv -w 1 does a port scan (zero-I/O, verbose, 1s timeout) rather than ICMP ping - useful when ICMP is blocked or you need to verify a specific service (e.g. SMB/445) is reachable across the subnet.

variations.label: Windows CMD
variations.description: Bash loop that pings a range of IP addresses for host discovery. Simple alternative to nmap -sn when specialized tools are unavailable.

variations.label: PowerShell
variations.description: PowerShell one-liner that pings all 254 addresses in a /24 subnet. Quick host discovery from a Windows foothold when nmap is not available.

variations.label: Meterpreter
variations.description: Runs a Metasploit post-exploitation module on an active session. Post modules automate common tasks like credential dumping, pivoting, and persistence.

recommended.note: Enumerate discovered hosts through the proxy.

defense.why_it_works: A ping sweep (Meterpreter post/multi/gather/ping_sweep, or a loop) discovers live hosts on the pivot's internal subnet to map the next targets.
defense.prerequisites: A foothold/session on a host with an internal-facing interface.
defense.impact: A list of live internal hosts - the map for further pivoting and attack.
defense.detection: [MITRE T1018] a burst of ICMP (or TCP) probes across an internal subnet sourced from the pivot; internal host-discovery pattern in east-west monitoring.
defense.artifacts: ICMP/ARP probes across the internal range from the pivot; the discovered host list.
defense.splunk_spl:
index=linux sourcetype="linux:auditd" comm="ping"
| stats dc(proctitle) as targets by host, bin(_time, 1m)
| where targets>20

index=network protocol=icmp
| stats dc(dest_ip) as hosts by src_ip | where hosts>20
defense.sentinel_kql:
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where RemoteIPType == "Private"
| summarize hosts=dcount(RemoteIP) by DeviceName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where hosts > 20
| sort by hosts desc
// a burst of probes across an internal subnet from the pivot
defense.sigma_rules: net_internal_ping_sweep_discovery (ICMP host discovery from the pivot - T1018)
defense.prevention: Internal segmentation and host-based firewalls; monitor east-west scanning; endpoint firewalls dropping unsolicited probes.
defense.evasion: Use ARP or targeted TCP probes over ICMP where ICMP is monitored; slow the sweep to avoid burst detection.
defense.misconfiguration: The network lacks proper segmentation - a compromised DMZ host has direct layer-3 reachability to internal infrastructure (database servers, DCs, internal admin panels). No egress filtering blocks outbound HTTP/HTTPS connections to arbitrary hosts, allowing C2 channels and reverse tunnels. Internal firewalls only filter inbound traffic, not east-west or outbound.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Network design: flat Layer-3 network, all VLANs can reach each other
# DMZ web server can ping/connect to: 10.10.10.0/24 (internal LAN), 10.10.20.0/24 (DB subnet)
# No egress proxy - direct outbound HTTP to any IP allowed

# iptables on pivot host (none blocking outbound):
iptables -L OUTPUT  # policy ACCEPT, no rules

# This allows: chisel client 10.10.10.5:8080 R:socks
# Attacker now has SOCKS5 access to the entire internal network
defense.secure_config:
# Network segmentation with explicit allow rules:
# DMZ -> Internet: only specific egress IPs (patch servers, DNS)
# DMZ -> Internal: ONLY the DB ports this specific app needs
# Internal -> Internal: segment by tier (web tier can't reach DC directly)

# Egress filtering - block all outbound except known-good:
# FortiGate / Palo Alto / iptables:
iptables -P OUTPUT DROP
iptables -A OUTPUT -d 8.8.8.8 -p udp --dport 53 -j ACCEPT  # DNS to specific server
iptables -A OUTPUT -p tcp --dport 443 -d <known_update_servers> -j ACCEPT
iptables -A OUTPUT -m state --state ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT

# IDS/IPS signatures for Chisel, ngrok, frp traffic patterns
# DNS monitoring - detect DNS tunneling (dnscat2) via unusual query frequency/length
# HTTP proxy with TLS inspection - detect reverse tunnels in HTTPS streams

validation.success_criteria: At least one behavioral detection fires within 60 seconds of attack execution
response_steps: Correlate alert with source host, user account, and timestamp
Review Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, Linux Audit (auditd), NetFlow / sFlow, Windows Security Event Log for surrounding context (5 min before/after)
Check for unusual network connections to/from the source host
Verify whether the activity matches known administrative baselines or change windows
If confirmed malicious, isolate the host and escalate to incident response
validation.test_command: for i in {1..254}; do (ping -c 1 172.16.5.$i | grep "bytes from" &); done

explain:
Sweeps an internal subnet for live hosts using only native shell tools, so no scanner upload is needed:
  for i in {1..254}   loop over every host in the /24
  ping -c 1 172.16.5.$i   send one ICMP echo to each
  grep "bytes from"       keep only the addresses that replied
  &                       background each ping so the sweep runs in parallel
Lists reachable internal hosts to target next; CMD, PowerShell, and the MSF ping_sweep module do the same on other footholds.
